Commentary.Commentary: We are back for the chase! The players are already out there. A big total to chase for Hong Kong, China, and their openers, Zeeshan Ali and Anshy Rath, need to deliver a quick start. Fazalhaq Farooqi to start proceedings with two slips in place. Here we go...
.... THE RUN CHASE ...

For Hong Kong, China, it was a tale of dropped catches and inexperience at the death. They started well with two early wickets, but spilling Sediqullah Atal in the first over, and twice more proved costly as he made them pay. A few other missed chances hurt too, showing the fine margins associate nations must master to compete with the big guns. They held things tight until the 16th over but then leaked runs like an open tap. Kinchit Shah was the standout with two wickets, and Ayush Shukla grabbed two but was expensive, while Ateeq Iqbal and Ehsan Khan chipped in with one each. Now their batters face a mammoth task against a fiery Afghan attack. Join us in a bit for the second essay!

The saving grace for Afghanistan was that Sediqullah Atal was still holding firm at the crease, and once Azmatullah Omarzai walked in, everything changed in a flash. The pair read the pitch beautifully and unleashed a stunning counterattack, sending the bowlers on a leather hunt. Atal brought up a well-deserved fifty, while Azmat rewrote history with the fastest T20I half-century by an Afghan batter, as the duo smacked 82 runs and piled on the misery of Hong Kong, China.

Afghanistan were rocked early, losing both Rahmanullah Gurbaz and Ibrahim Zadran and finding themselves in real trouble. But the decision to send in Mohammad Nabi proved a masterstroke - he blended calm composure with flashes of aggression to steady the innings. At the other end, Sediqullah Atal capitalised on the early reprieve he got in the first over, growing in confidence as the partnership blossomed. The duo stitched together a vital 51-run stand before Nabi’s departure, after which Afghanistan’s momentum dipped slightly, and they found themselves grinding through a tricky phase post halfway stage.

A batting effort of two contrasting halves! Afghanistan looked scratchy early on, struggling to find their rhythm, but their seasoned campaigners steadied the ship through the middle overs. And then came the fireworks - Azmat lit up the stadium with a breathtaking maiden T20I fifty off just 20 balls, sending the crowd into a frenzy. The Afghans went absolutely ballistic at the death, hammering 69 runs in the final 4 overs to storm their way to a mammoth total.
Nails in a yorker around middle and leg, does Ehsan. Atal creates room for himself and carves it to the right of the bowler for a single. 9 runs from the final over! AFGHANISTAN FINISH AT 188/6!

Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS. Quite a sweaty first half of the first inning, to say the least. It is still really warm out there. From Hong Kong, China's perspective, they have not let the Afghans run away with the score and have kept things decently quiet. Bowling stump-to-stump has prevented the batters from playing freely. And from Afghanistan's point of view, after losing two big wickets inside the Powerplay, they have steadied the ship convincingly. Mohammad Nabi and Sediqullah Atal have respected the conditions and haven't tried anything risky as yet, and have constructed a solid partnership for the third wicket. Either one of these two will need to bat till the end for a big score on the board. The wicket seems slowish in nature, but with the ball softening up, batting has appeared to be a bit breathable. Hong Kong, China will need to break this blossoming partnership ASAP. A bowling change after the hydration break. Kinchit Shah is into the attack.

Commentary.Commentary: All set for the curtain raiser of the 17th edition of the Asia Cup to begin. Fair to say, it is very warm out there, with the temperature in the late thirties as we speak. We can see the jerseys flapping so that indicates it is a bit windy as well. The umpires and players have made their way out to the middle. Yasim Murtaza leads his men out as Hong Kong, China's players spread out to the field to take their respective positions. For Afghanistan, it will be the opening pair of Sediqullah Atal and Rahmanullah Gurbaz, the same pair that opened for them in the recently concluded tri-series in Sharjah. Ayush Shukla has the new ball and will begin the proceedings. Atal to face. The countdown is done and 'Let's Play' says the umpire.

Just a few minutes away from the action to begin in Abu Dhabi. But before that, both sets of players, followed by the match officials, are lining up for their respective national anthems. It will be Hong Kong, China's first, followed by the national anthem of Afghanistan.
Hong Kong, China (Playing XI) - Zeeshan Ali (WK), Babar Hayat, Anshy Rath, Kalhan Challu, Nizakat Khan, Aizaz Khan, Kinchit Shah, Yasim Murtaza (C), Ayush Shukla, Ateeq Iqbal, Ehsan Khan.

Afghanistan (Playing XI) - Rahmanullah Gurbaz (WK), Ibrahim Zadran, Sediqullah Atal, Azmatullah Omarzai, Mohammad Nabi, Karim Janat, Gulbadin Naib, Rashid Khan (C), Noor Ahmad, AM Ghazanfar, Fazalhaq Farooqi.

PITCH REPORT - Bazid Khan is pitchside. He says that there is a lot of grass, but is a mix between live and dead grass. Adds that both spinners and seamers will get help. Russell Arnold joins him and says that batting first is a good option as dew won't be much of a factor here. Ends by saying that 180 was the average first innings score in ILT20, so that should be the target.

The captain of Hong Kong, China, Yasim Murtaza, says that they would have batted first as well, but don't mind bowling first either. Reflects that they had a tough battle against Oman before getting into this competition, but also points out that they played really good cricket. Says he is looking forward to how Kalhan Challu performs. Mentions that he is a very talented player, and as a team, he says they are looking to perform well on a big stage.

The captain of Afghanistan, Rashid Khan, says they will bat first. Adds that it looks like a good wicket and they would like to put a good score on the board. Mentions that they have a good bowling group, but it is not just about the spinners. Says that they have put the Tri-Series final behind them, it was good preparation, and they have had discussions on how to improve on that. Ends by saying that even if they had won the final, they would not change their style of playing.
TOSS UPDATE - The flip of the coin lands in favor of Afghanistan and skipper Rashid Khan elects to BAT first.

So, overall, Afghanistan do enter as the favorites, but Hong Kong, China does hold the calibre to surprise them with a knockout punch at the start of the tournament. The festival of Asian Cricket and the battle of supremacy over the region is about to begin. Stay tuned for the toss and the playing XI.

Speaking about the Hong Kong, China side, they have an outside chance of starting the tournament with a big upset and repeating their 2015 heroics against the same team at the same venue. Yasim Murtaza will look to lead the team right from the front and deliver an all-around performance in this contest. Their biggest hope lies in the hands of their openers, Anshy Rath and Zeeshan Ali, and of course, their premier batter, Babar Hayat, to continue their good form with the bat and score some valuable runs. The player to keep an eye on with the ball will be Ayush Shukla, who will try to exploit the Afghan batters' vulnerability and scalp some quick early wickets.

Coming into this tournament as one of the favourites, Afghanistan would be vulnerable after their recent defeat in the UAE Tri-Series finale against Pakistan. They would look to forget that humbling loss and start afresh their campaign. They do have specific concerns they would like to address in this contest, and the biggest one is the unsettled form of their star batter, Rahmanullah Gurbaz. Due to this, they will heavily rely on Sediqullah Atal and Ibrahim Zadran to do most of the hard work in their batting lineup. Another vulnerability has been the so-so form of their middle order, which will be put to test as the challenges get elevated. Amongst the bowlers, like the usual thing, spinners do have the responsibility of turning the game in their team's favour. And as a team, the Afghans would look to tick off some boxes from this contest and move forward in this tournament with some positives.

Hello, and a warm welcome to everyone joining us for the first match of the Men's T20 Asia Cup 2025, which will see Afghanistan and Hong Kong, China clash at Zayed Cricket Stadium in Abu Dhabi. This is the third time the Asia Cup is being contested in the T20I format, following the 2016 and 2022 editions. India enter the tournament as the defending champions. Also, for the first time, eight teams are taking part, the highest number in any Asia Cup, with the sides split into two groups of four. Also, this is the one and only multinational competition before next year's T20 World Cup, scheduled to be hosted in India and Sri Lanka. In a historic moment, this edition also marks Oman’s maiden appearance in the Asia Cup.
... MATCH DAY ...

East meets West, spin meets spirit - that’s the flavour as the Asia Cup 2025 begins with Afghanistan taking on Hong Kong, China in the opening clash at the Zayed Cricket Stadium in Abu Dhabi. It’s the start of a tournament that has grown into Asia’s own festival of cricket. For the first time, eight teams are part of the Asia Cup, up from six in the previous edition, and it’s all in the fast-paced T20I format, keeping the 2026 T20 World Cup, scheduled to be held in India and Sri Lanka, in mind. India may remain the official host, but because of tensions with Pakistan, the entire event is shifted to the UAE, where cricket has become a second home for many Asian teams. With Group B already being called the ‘group of death’, featuring Afghanistan, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh alongside Hong Kong, China, every match could decide survival. Let’s know about Afghanistan first. They are a team that has transformed from a plucky underdog to a genuine powerhouse. For them, this match is about momentum. They come into the tournament bruised, having been bundled out for just 66 in the Tri-Series final against Pakistan. That defeat exposed their fragile batting, but if there’s one thing Afghanistan have shown over the years, it’s RESILIENCE. Under Rashid Khan’s captaincy, they now look more polished and dangerous than ever. Rashid himself had a poor IPL but rediscovered his rhythm with the Oval Invincibles in the Hundred and followed it up with 9 wickets, including a fiery three-wicket spell in the Tri-Series final, which also marked his 100th T20I. The spin cartel of Rashid, Mujeeb Ur Rahman, Mohammad Nabi, Noor Ahmad, and newcomer AM Ghazanfar is easily one of the strongest in world cricket, tailor-made for the UAE’s slow tracks. Add the pace of Fazalhaq Farooqi and Naveen-ul-Haq, with Azmatullah Omarzai and Gulbadin Naib offering balance, and Afghanistan’s bowling looks like a juggernaut. But it’s their batting that needs to step up. Ibrahim Zadran’s return was a huge plus in the Tri-Series, where he struck a couple of fifties. Alongside Sediqullah Atal, who also contributed two fifties in that tournament, they provide some firepower at the top of the order. Rahmanullah Gurbaz, known for his explosive batting, adds further strength, and if all these players perform well, any team could be in trouble. Veteran Mohammad Nabi and all-rounder Karim Janat add depth, but consistency remains the biggest concern. They tasted their best-ever T20I World Cup run in 2024, reaching the semi-finals, but the challenge for Afghanistan will be to convert their potential into a major title win, a feat they have yet to achieve despite their undeniable talent and a strong build-up to this tournament. To get there, they need to shed the tag of being a ‘spin-dependent’ side and prove they can put runs on the board. For Hong Kong, China, the journey is about BELIEF. They return for their fifth Asia Cup appearance and second in the T20I format, still hunting for their first-ever win in the tournament. Their rise here came through the ACC Men’s Premier Cup, where they finished as one of the top three Associate Nations, including Oman and the UAE. A new era begins under captain Yasim Murtaza and coach Kaushal Silva, the former Sri Lanka cricketer, who has just taken charge. Their preparation has been challenging, with the team relying on a two-week crash course in Dubai after months of being confined to indoor nets. Despite these hurdles, they have a squad with a familiar and experienced core. They aren’t short of talent - Anshy Rath, with an average of over 50 in T20Is this year, has been their most consistent batter, while the experienced Babar Hayat, the only batter other than Virat Kohli to score a century in an Asia Cup T20I, brings firepower. Nizakat Khan and the explosive Zeeshan Ali round out a formidable top four capable of competing against any team. Their bowling is their secret weapon. Ehsan Khan, the off-spinner, is among the most effective bowlers in Associate cricket. Skipper Murtaza adds left-arm spin, and together they will love the UAE’s turning surfaces. Then there’s Ayush Shukla, the 22-year-old pacer who grabbed headlines in 2024 by bowling four maidens in a T20I - a world record feat. Add names like Ateeq Iqbal, Nasrulla Rana, and Kalhan Challu, and Hong Kong, China may lack big names, but they are well-drilled. Still, their biggest concern is the lack of match practice against top-tier teams. Talking about the conditions, which could level things a little, the UAE’s pitches in the recent UAE Tri-Series showed a strange trend, where all 7 matches, including the final, were won by the team batting first, often by one-sided margins. Totals of 170-plus were challenging, but the batters can hit through the line effectively. Spinners still found grip and turn, and this all makes the toss extremely crucial, and both teams will eye batting first. Also, due to the UAE heat, 18 of the 19 matches will start at 6.30 pm local time (2.30 pm GMT), a half-hour pushback from the original schedule. Head-to-head, the two sides last met in the first round of the 2016 T20I World Cup, where Afghanistan were victorious, but their most recent encounter in an ODI in the ICC Cricket World Cup Qualifier in 2018 went to Hong Kong, China. The tournament format will see the top two teams from each group - Group A (India, Oman, Pakistan, and UAE) and Group B (Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Hong Kong, China, and Sri Lanka) - advance to a four-team ‘Super 4' group. The top two teams at the end of the Super 4 stage will then face off in the final on September 28. India are the defending champions of the 2023 ODI edition, while Sri Lanka claimed the previous T20I edition in 2022. While the teams have not faced off in a T20I for a while, Afghanistan, who treat the UAE as a home away from home, will still start as favourites, but Hong Kong, China, desperate to make history, could spring a surprise if their senior batters fire and their spinners choke the Afghan middle order. The stage is set - a spin-heavy Afghanistan gunning for glory against a spirited Hong Kong, China, chasing their first win. The desert evenings in Abu Dhabi have a way of producing drama, and with the Asia Cup now an eight-team festival, this opener could very well set the tone for the entire tournament.
